title: HE WAS A WANTED MAN WITH NOTHING LEFT. THEN SEVEN SISTERS WALKED INTO HIS STORY.
paragraphs: HE WAS A WANTED MAN WITH NOTHING LEFT. THEN SEVEN SISTERS WALKED INTO HIS STORY.

Before Moses ever stood before Pharaoh to deliver a nation, he stood beside a well to defend seven women. He thought he had lost his future. But in the wilderness, God was preparing a chapter he never saw coming.
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” — Exodus 2:21 (KJV)
What if the worst chapter of your life is not the final chapter God will write?
What if the place you never wanted to be becomes the place where God begins teaching you who you were created to become?
And what if the moment that changes your future arrives on an ordinary day, when nobody is watching, nobody is applauding, and you have absolutely nothing to gain?
Because before Moses became the man who confronted Pharaoh, before the Red Sea opened, before the burning bush, before the thunder of Mount Sinai...
He was a fugitive.
A frightened man.
A stranger in a foreign land.
And one day, he found himself sitting beside a well.
He had no idea that seven sisters were about to enter his story.
He certainly had no idea that one of them would become his wife.
But to understand what happened at that well, you must first understand what Moses was carrying when he arrived there.
Because this was not the Moses we remember from Sunday school.
This was Moses before the miracles.
Before the calling became clear.
Before his life made sense.
And that is precisely why this story matters to anyone who has ever wondered whether God can still do something beautiful with a life that has gone terribly wrong.
Moses had grown up in Pharaoh's household, surrounded by privileges most Israelites could never imagine.
Yet he belonged to a suffering people.
Exodus 2:11 tells us that when Moses had grown, he went out to his own people and saw their burdens.
He witnessed an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
And Moses intervened.
But what happened next was not an act of righteous restraint.
It was a killing.
Scripture says Moses looked this way and that, saw no one, killed the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
Read that carefully.
He looked around.
He killed.
He hid the body.
This is not a detail we should soften simply because Moses later became a great servant of God.
The Bible does not need us to make its heroes look innocent.
It tells the truth about human failure because the grace of God is powerful enough to meet sinners in the truth.
The next day, Moses tried to intervene in a dispute between two Hebrews.
But one of them confronted him with words that must have pierced straight through his confidence.
“Who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian?” — Exodus 2:14 (KJV)
His secret was no longer secret.
And when Pharaoh heard what had happened, he sought to kill Moses.
So Moses fled.
Imagine the weight of that journey.
The life he had known was behind him.
The consequences of his actions were following him.
And the future ahead was uncertain.
Scripture does not tell us every thought that passed through his mind. We should not pretend to know them.
But it tells us enough to understand that Moses had lost his place in Egypt and was now living as a stranger.
Then comes a sentence so quiet that you could almost miss its significance.
“But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian: and he sat down by a well.” — Exodus 2:15 (KJV)
He sat down by a well.
Not on a throne.
Not in a palace.
Not before an audience.
At a well.
And sometimes the most important moments in a person's life begin in places that appear completely ordinary.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיֵּשֶׁב בְּאֶרֶץ־מִדְיָן וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל־הַבְּאֵר
Vayyeshev be'erets Midyan, vayyeshev al-habbe'er.
“He settled in the land of Midian, and he sat by the well.”
The Hebrew verb vayyeshev comes from יָשַׁב (yashav), which can mean to sit, dwell, or settle, depending on its context.
The repetition is striking.
Moses settled in Midian.
Moses sat beside a well.
A man whose life had been thrown into upheaval had arrived somewhere he could stop.
But the text does not say he knew what would happen next.
Then seven women approached.
They were the daughters of the priest of Midian, and they had come to draw water for their father's flock.
This was work.
Ordinary, necessary, daily work.
They were not arriving for a dramatic encounter.
They were caring for animals.
They drew water and filled the troughs.
And then something happened.
The shepherds came and drove them away.
Imagine doing the work required of you, only to have someone stronger push you aside.
Imagine being treated as though your effort meant nothing.
Imagine the exhaustion of having to defend your place when all you came to do was complete an honest day's labor.
The Bible does not explain the shepherds' motives, but it makes their actions clear.
They drove the women away.
And Moses saw it.
Here is where the story becomes extraordinary.
Because Moses had already experienced what happened when he responded to injustice with deadly violence.
He was now a foreigner, without the security of Pharaoh's household.
He could have remained seated.
He could have decided that these women's problems were none of his concern.
He could have told himself that he had already lost enough by getting involved in other people's suffering.
But he did not remain seated.
Exodus 2:17 says:
“And the shepherds came and drove them away: but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.” (KJV)
Moses stood up.
Those three words carry the turning point of the scene.
The Hebrew says:
וַיָּקָם מֹשֶׁה וַיּוֹשִׁעָן
Vayyaqom Mosheh vayyoshi'an.
“And Moses arose and delivered them.”
The verb translated “delivered” or “rescued” comes from the Hebrew root יָשַׁע (yasha), associated with saving, helping, or delivering.
That matters.
Moses did not merely offer sympathetic words from a distance.
He acted.
He defended the women and watered their flock.
And notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Moses knew these women had a father who would invite him home.
It does not say Moses knew one of them would become his wife.
It does not say he expected payment, recognition, or a reward.
The passage presents a man responding to a wrong before any personal benefit is mentioned.
There is a lesson here that our generation desperately needs.
Not every good thing you do will be noticed.
Not every act of courage will receive applause.
Not every person you help will remember your name.
And not every faithful decision will lead to an immediate reward.
But doing what is right does not become meaningless simply because nobody promises you anything in return.
Sometimes integrity is revealed most clearly when there is nothing obvious to gain.
And sometimes the person God is shaping in private matters more than the reputation we are trying to build in public.
Moses did not yet know that he would one day be called to lead Israel out of Egypt.
But here, beside a well, we see a man who could not simply watch the vulnerable be pushed aside.
That does not erase his earlier sin.
It does not mean he had become perfect.
And the Bible does not say that defending these women earned him God's forgiveness.
But the scene allows us to see something important about his character.
His past failure was real.
Yet that failure was not the only truth about his life.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that matters.
Because you have made decisions you cannot undo.
You have spoken words you wish you could take back.
You have hurt someone.
You have disappointed people who believed in you.
Perhaps you have disappointed yourself.
And somewhere along the way, you began to believe that your worst moment had become your permanent identity.
But Scripture does not teach that repentance is impossible for those who have fallen.
It teaches that sinners need the mercy of God.
The same Bible that records Moses' killing of the Egyptian also records the extraordinary work God later accomplished through him.
And the New Testament makes the foundation of our hope even clearer.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7 (KJV)
Our forgiveness is not purchased by doing enough good deeds to outweigh our failures.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement that the Son of God came to save sinners, died for our sins, and rose again.
And those who turn to Him in faith are not left to carry the guilt of their past as though His cross accomplished nothing.
Now return to that well.
The seven sisters went home.
And their father noticed something unusual.
They had returned earlier than expected.
Exodus 2:18 records his question:
“How is it that ye are come so soon to day?” (KJV)
Their answer reveals something beautiful.
“An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock.” — Exodus 2:19 (KJV)
An Egyptian.
That is how they described Moses.
They did not introduce him as Israel's future deliverer.
They did not know the full story of the man who had helped them.
They simply knew that a stranger had intervened when they needed help.
And their father immediately asked a question.
“And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread.” — Exodus 2:20 (KJV)
Do not rush past that.
A man who had fled from Pharaoh was now being invited into someone's home.
A stranger was being offered hospitality.
A man whose future was uncertain was being given a place at a table.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Because sometimes what a weary person needs is not a grand speech.
Sometimes it is a door opened.
A meal offered.
A place to sit.
A reminder that they have not become invisible.

The father is later identified as Reuel in Exodus 2:18, while other passages associate Moses' father-in-law with the name Jethro. Scripture uses both names in connection with Moses' Midianite family, although interpreters discuss the precise relationship between the names.
And then comes the moment that inspired this entire story.
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” — Exodus 2:21 (KJV)
Her name was Zipporah.
The Hebrew is צִפֹּרָה — Tsipporah, commonly understood to be related to the Hebrew word tsippor, meaning “bird.”
The passage does not describe the moment Moses first spoke to her privately.
It does not tell us whether they immediately felt attracted to one another.
It does not give us a romantic conversation beside the water.
And it certainly does not tell us that Moses defended the seven sisters because he was looking for a wife.
We must resist the temptation to invent details that Scripture has not given us.
The beauty of this story is already powerful enough without adding imaginary scenes.
Moses defended seven women.
Their father welcomed him.
Moses agreed to stay.
And Zipporah became his wife.
Think about that sequence.
He did not arrive in Midian searching for a marriage.
He arrived because he was fleeing for his life.
He did not stand up against the shepherds because he knew the outcome.
He stood up when he saw women being mistreated.
And the relationship that eventually brought Zipporah into his life unfolded in the very place where Moses had come as an exile.
But here is something we need to be careful about.
This story is not a promise that every good deed will lead to marriage.
It is not a guarantee that if you defend someone, God will reward you with a spouse.
And it is not biblical to tell every lonely person that their future husband or wife is waiting beside some metaphorical well.
That may sound inspirational.
But it would go beyond what God has actually said.
The deeper truth is far more enduring.
Your circumstances do not place you beyond God's reach.
You may be somewhere you never planned to be.
You may be starting over at an age when you thought everything would already be settled.
You may be watching other people celebrate milestones while you are still trying to understand what happened to your own dreams.
You may be carrying grief that nobody sees.
And perhaps you have asked God a question you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Lord, is there still anything good ahead of me?”
Moses' story does not give us permission to predict exactly what God will do next in your life.
But it does remind us that the God of Scripture is not limited by the circumstances that overwhelm us.
And the greatest evidence of that truth is not a marriage beside a well.
It is a Savior who walked out of a tomb.
Because the Gospel tells us that even death itself could not defeat the purpose of God accomplished through Jesus Christ.
The story of Moses and Zipporah becomes even more meaningful when we remember that marriage was not the end of Moses' wilderness journey.
Their son Gershom was born.
Moses explained his son's name by saying:
“I have been a stranger in a strange land.” — Exodus 2:22 (KJV)
The Hebrew name גֵּרְשֹׁם — Gershom is connected in the narrative to Moses' experience of living as a foreigner.
Even after receiving a home and a family, Moses remembered that he was a stranger.
Isn't that painfully human?
Sometimes your life changes, but the memory of what you have been through remains.
You can find a place to belong and still remember what it felt like to be displaced.
You can experience love and still carry the scars of rejection.
You can receive mercy and still remember the consequences of your mistakes.
Healing does not always mean forgetting.
And God's work in a person's life does not require pretending the past never happened.
Years later, Moses would encounter God at the burning bush while tending the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law.
The man who once sat beside a well in Midian would eventually stand before Pharaoh with a message from the Lord.
But the years between those moments were real.
The waiting was real.
The ordinary work was real.
The wilderness was not a short interruption before an instant triumph.
Moses spent many years there.
And that should comfort those who are weary of waiting.
Because the Bible does not present spiritual maturity as something that always develops overnight.
God's people often learn obedience through seasons they would never have chosen.
Yet we must not confuse waiting with abandonment.
Exodus 2 ends by telling us that God heard the groaning of the Israelites, remembered His covenant, looked upon His people, and knew their condition.
God had not forgotten His covenant.
Even while Moses was living in Midian, the Lord's purposes for Israel had not disappeared.
And when God called Moses, the calling did not come because Moses had finally become a flawless hero.
In fact, Moses expressed fear and reluctance.
He questioned his ability.
He struggled with the responsibility.
The God who called him was greater than the weakness of the man being called.
That is where this story begins to point us toward something even greater than Moses.
Because Moses was a deliverer, but he was not the final Deliverer.
Moses could confront Pharaoh.
But he could not remove the guilt of humanity's sin.
Moses could lead Israel through the sea.
But he could not, by his own power, bring sinners into eternal life.
Moses was a servant in God's house.
Jesus Christ is the Son over God's house.
Hebrews 3:5–6 draws that distinction.
And John 1:17 tells us:
“For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
The Bible is not inviting us merely to admire Moses' courage.
It is leading us toward the God who fulfills His saving purposes in Christ.
Consider another encounter at a well.
Centuries after Moses sat in Midian, Jesus sat beside Jacob's well in Samaria.
A woman came to draw water.
She had a complicated personal history.
And Jesus spoke to her.
He did not treat her as someone beyond the reach of truth and mercy.
He exposed what needed to be brought into the light.
And He offered something no earthly well could provide.
“Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst.” — John 4:14 (KJV)
The encounters are not identical, and Scripture does not explicitly declare the Midian well to be a prophecy of the Samaritan well.
But reading them together reveals a beautiful contrast.
At one well, Moses helped women receive the water they needed for their flock.
At another well, Jesus offered living water that leads to eternal life.
Moses was a man in need of God's mercy.
Jesus is the Savior who gives mercy to sinners.
Moses found a home in a foreign land.
Through Christ, those who were once far off are brought near to God.
And perhaps that is the message somebody desperately needs to hear today.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect past before coming to Jesus.
You do not have to pretend that your sins were harmless.
You do not have to hide behind religious appearances.
You can confess what is true.
You can repent.
You can come to Christ.
Because the cross is not a celebration of sin.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the astonishing love of God meet.
Jesus did not die to make rebellion against God seem insignificant.
He died to save sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
So if you are reading this while carrying a secret shame, hear the invitation of Scripture.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
You are not being invited to excuse your past.
You are being invited to bring it into the light of Christ.
And if you have already trusted Jesus but still feel trapped by memories of who you used to be, remember that your identity is not defined solely by your worst failure.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It means that union with Christ brings a new life that your past sins cannot produce and your own efforts cannot purchase.
And now, perhaps, you can see why the story of Moses and the seven sisters is so much more than an unusual account of how a man met his future wife.
It is a story about a fugitive who still had the capacity to act courageously.
A story about women whose mistreatment was not ignored.
A story about hospitality offered to a stranger.
A story about a marriage that began during an unexpected season of exile.
And within the larger story of Exodus, it is part of the journey of a man whom God would later call to serve in the deliverance of Israel.
There is no need to turn Moses into a perfect romantic hero.
There is no need to turn Zipporah into a prize for good behavior.
She was a real woman, part of a real family, whose life became intertwined with Moses' life.
And their marriage would have its own difficult moments, as Exodus 4:24–26 reminds us.
The Bible does not present their relationship as a flawless fairy tale.
It presents real people within the unfolding history of God's covenant purposes.
That is what makes Scripture so trustworthy and so relevant.
It does not hide the complications of human life.
It tells the truth.
And it leads us to the One who is truly able to redeem.
So the next time you feel tempted to believe that your life is over because something went wrong, remember the man sitting beside a well in Midian.
Remember that he did not know what the future held.
Remember that the next right thing in front of him was simply to help people who were being treated unjustly.
And remember that his future was not revealed to him all at once.
Perhaps your next act of faithfulness will not look dramatic either.
Perhaps it will be telling the truth when lying would be easier.
Apologizing without making excuses.
Refusing to exploit someone weaker than you.
Showing kindness to a person who cannot repay you.
Remaining faithful to Christ when the applause has disappeared.
Or finally surrendering a sin you have spent years trying to conceal.
Do not do these things because you expect God to owe you a reward.
Do them because Jesus Christ is worthy of your obedience.
And when you fall short, return to Him in repentance and faith.
The Gospel is not that good people earn beautiful endings.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and make them new.
That is the grace that rewrites everything.
And I want to ask you something personal.
What is the “Midian” in your life right now?
Is it a season of starting over?
A broken relationship?
A mistake you are still trying to make right?
A lonely place where you wonder whether God sees you?
Or perhaps you are standing at a different kind of well, facing an opportunity to do what is right even though nobody is watching.
Whatever your answer, do not underestimate the spiritual importance of the ordinary choices in front of you.
Not because every act of obedience guarantees a visible blessing.
But because faithfulness matters to God even when the world never notices.
You do not need to explain your entire struggle publicly. Sometimes those three words are enough to let fellow believers know you need encouragement.
Your story may encourage someone who has almost given up hope.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message today.
Someone who believes one terrible decision has disqualified them forever.
Someone who has been pushed aside, forgotten, or mistreated.
Someone who is trying to find the courage to start again.
Not because following a page makes anyone more righteous.
But because what we continually read, hear, and meditate upon can help shape the direction of our hearts.

We want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where the broken are pointed toward Christ, the weary are encouraged by Scripture, the wandering are called to repentance, and believers are challenged to grow in truth and grace.
Every article, devotional, and discipleship resource takes time, effort, and ongoing support to develop and share.

Scripture teaches the importance of generous, willing support for Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 encourages believers to share good things with those who teach them the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or forced, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But if the Lord has given you the desire and the means to help this ministry continue, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
These products are not the heart of our ministry.
Jesus is.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed with Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to build a community that treasures Jesus Christ.
A community that knows grace is not permission to remain in sin, but the power of God that teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live for Him.
A community that knows biblical truth can confront us without destroying our hope.
A community that refuses to give up on people whom Christ is calling to repentance and new life.
Before you leave, return with me one final time to that well.
A man sits alone in a foreign land.
Seven sisters approach with their flock.
The shepherds drive them away.
The stranger stands.
He helps them.
He waters their animals.
And the women return home with a story about an Egyptian who defended them.
A father opens his door.
A stranger receives hospitality.
And in time, Moses marries Zipporah.
There is no thunder from heaven in this scene.
No sea dividing.
No pillar of fire.
No voice from a burning bush.
Just a man, a well, seven sisters, and an unexpected act of courage.
Yet this quiet episode belongs to the same biblical story in which God would later bring His people out of slavery.
And that is worth remembering when your own life feels painfully ordinary.
You do not know every chapter ahead.
You do not know how long the wilderness will last.
You do not know which doors will open or which hopes will have to be surrendered.
But you can know the One who calls sinners to Himself.
You can know the Savior who died and rose again.
You can know the grace that does not deny your sin but offers forgiveness through His blood.
And you can trust Him enough to take the next faithful step.
Moses' story began long before he met Zipporah, and it did not end when he married her.
Your life is bigger than one failure, one relationship, one disappointment, or one season of waiting.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest hope is not that every earthly dream will come true.
It is that the One who saved you will never abandon His redemptive purpose for you.
So stand for what is right.
Love without demanding a reward.
Repent when you sin.
Receive the mercy of Christ.
And do not mistake an unfinished chapter for the end of the story.
The wilderness may be where you lost the life you expected, but it does not have to be where you lose your hope in the God who saves.
